rows.evidence: Q1: Methods sections 2.1-2.3 and Table 2 report the authors' own LPJmL model runs (688 simulations) of water management scenarios.
rows.notes: The study is a global scenario simulation. Drip appears only inside combined irrigation-transition scenarios ('best practice' = drip where suitable plus sprinkler; 'all drip'), with system efficiencies taken as parameters from J<U+00E4>germeyr et al 2015. The simulated reductions in consumptive irrigation losses (24/48/85%, section 3.2) and withdrawal cuts are scenario outputs that are never compared with measurements of real drip systems; only the baseline run is calibrated to FAO national yields and compared with other withdrawal estimates (section 3.6). Under the rule that a model counts only when its output on the claimed effect is checked against observations, this is rated 'no', with the doubt noted that the baseline is calibrated. The study also notes (3.6) that upstream irrigation improvements can reduce return flows downstream.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods sections 2.1-2.3 and Table 2 report the authors' own LPJmL model runs of water management scenarios.
rows.notes: The study reports no result on river flows, environmental flows or aquatic ecosystems under drip. It only models kcal production, transpiration coefficient, irrigation withdrawal/consumption and the water gap. Where it touches river flows (section 3.6, discussion) it states that upstream irrigation and water-harvesting interventions can reduce return flows and runoff and negatively affect downstream water availability, and that environmental flow requirements should be respected <U+2014> i.e. not evidence of enhanced river flows sustaining ecosystems. Modeled results are also not compared with observations.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods sections 2.1-2.3 and Table 2 report the authors' own LPJmL model runs; section 3.3 reports the simulated 7/26/43% global kcal increases from irrigation improvement plus expansion with saved water.
rows.notes: The 26% figure the review cites is indeed reported (section 3.3, 'ambitious' IRRexp scenario: 'best practice' irrigation = drip where suitable plus sprinkler, with saved water used to expand irrigation into rainfed land). However it is a scenario simulation whose output on the claimed drip effect is not compared with measurements; the only checks are baseline calibration to FAO yields and a qualitative comparison of water-harvesting/mulching yield gains with case studies (section 3.6), not of irrigation-system transitions. Drip is also not isolated from sprinkler and from irrigation expansion in the 26% number. Rated 'no' on Q2 with this doubt recorded; climate ensemble (20 GCMs) and sensitivity analyses exist but are irrelevant once Q2 is 'no'.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references; supplementary figures S1-S5 and tables S1-S2 not included). The study is a global LPJmL modeling exercise; drip irrigation is one component of combined scenarios rather than a separately evaluated technology, and no scenario output is validated against field observations of drip systems.
